name: Physically isolated Micrologic flip-flop
summary: Fairchild's first working one-piece silicon flip-flop kept its transistors apart with etched, epoxy-filled channels, a method soon dropped for junction isolation.
description: Fairchild’s physically isolated monolithic four-transistor flip-flop design, including rear-etched epoxy-filled channels; distinct from the later junction-isolated implementation and not identified with an initial Type F sale.
tier_reason: A bounded technical contribution, transmission episode or documented configuration useful within a specific history; no broad dependence claim is established.

date.basis: The cited account dates this scoped event to the stated interval.

events.statement: Lionel Kattner recalled that Fairchild decided at the end of 1960 to phase out physically isolated Phase Two and concentrate on junction-isolated Phase Three.
events.scope: Fairchild Phase Two physically isolated Micrologic development.
events.caveats: This is a retrospective recollection of a decision, not proof that a shutdown was completed on that date or that all physically isolated circuits ceased. Last separately recalled a December 1960 memo still weighing both approaches; customer/sample recollections also differ.

evidence.locator: Printed pp. 17–18: Kattner, Last and Norman panel discussion
evidence.supports: Kattner recalled a decision at the end of 1960 to phase out physically isolated Phase Two and concentrate on junction-isolated Phase Three; Last recalled a December 1960 decision remained open.

date.label: 26 May 1960
date.basis: The museum chronology dates the first working physically isolated monolithic circuit to 26 May; Jay Last independently places the relevant sample in May. The exact day relies on a retrospective institutional account.

events.statement: Last’s team produced a working physically isolated monolithic Micrologic flip-flop.
events.scope: Physically isolated four-transistor Norman flip-flop development device, with rear-etched epoxy-filled channels.
events.caveats: The exact day is retrospective; no original fabrication notebook was inspected. This specimen is not equated with the first sold Type F die.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 84; Jay Last chronology; PDF p. 132 mask layout
evidence.supports: Documents first working physically isolated Micrologic flip-flop in May 1960 and distinguishes later versions.

date.basis: Date of this documented community-facing use, recognition, or communication; not a claim of first occurrence.

events.statement: Life published a Micrologic photograph on 10 March 1961; later museum and participant accounts identify the pictured sample as physically isolated.
events.scope: Photographed Micrologic flip-flop sample later identified by participants and the museum as physically isolated; this scope concerns its visual exposure, not disclosure of the rear-etched epoxy method.
events.caveats: The identification of the photographed device as physically isolated is retrospective. The original Life article and caption were not inspected, and readers are not shown to have learned the rear-etched epoxy method. The photographed sample is not established as the first-working May die or a sold Type F die.

evidence.locator: Printed p. 22, March 10 Life photograph and retrospective museum caption
evidence.supports: Reproduces a photograph identified retrospectively by the museum as a physically isolated Micrologic sample and dates its appearance in Life.
The participant chronology identifies an earlier physically isolated device in the Life photograph.

evidence.locator: Printed p. 33, March 1961 chronology; p. 25, Last discussing the Life photograph
evidence.supports: Identifies the 10 March Life image as an earlier physically isolated device.
Confirms that the image showed an epoxy-isolated device in a TO-18 can.

community_entry.proxy_reason: Readers could see a photograph of a device later identified as physically isolated; this does not establish that the article explained its hidden isolation method, that readers understood that method, customer use or a sale.

caveats: The May specimen, the photographed March 1961 sample, and the first sold Type F die are not established as the same physical object or mask.

links.statement: Last’s project implemented the monolithic approach specified by Noyce’s patent.
links.alternatives: The project’s first multi-chip demonstration preceded the monolithic device.
links.caveats: The fabricated isolation method is recorded separately from the patent’s illustrative structures.
links.timing: July 1959 filing precedes project initiation and 1960 implementation.

evidence.supports: Noyce patent named as project basis.

links.statement: Last’s IC project explicitly used Hoerni’s planar process to fabricate its circuit components.
links.scope: Fairchild project initiated August 1959; May 1960 monolithic implementation.
links.alternatives: The team first demonstrated a multi-chip circuit; Kilby used separate wired elements.
links.caveats: Circuit design and isolation required additional work beyond making a planar transistor.
links.timing: March transistor precedes the August project and May 1960 circuit.

evidence.supports: Project basis and working physical-isolation circuit.
